reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes paid BitClub participation through a $99 membership payment and claims that accounts, team expansion, and strategically placed multiple accounts can generate passive earnings. It presents credit thresholds, salaries, bonuses, branching payouts, and earnings of up to $2,000 daily per account as benefits of the paid structure. The material does not independently verify the mining activity, actual payouts, participant losses, or whether the illustrated earnings were achieved.

citations.quote: Pool 1 will cost you $500. It will be valued at 3 credits
For every participation in the pool, the Bitglod physically acquires IT hardware that will be integrated in our mining facilities.
The Cycle Bonus generates Bitcoins for worth $200 per cycle.
Our club system is based on a binary structure.
Once you've added 15 credits, which is equivalent to $2,500 in both teams, you'll get a $200 salary

opening.argument: Judge the earnings language by what it actually commits to. The largest daily figure is conditional: the narration says a member “may even increase” cycles by taking a particular position in the system, then describes what that “would” bring in [ASR_0002]. Its worked example begins “Let's say” [ASR_0003]. Those qualifications do not make the figures reliable, but they matter: this is an explanation of a proposed calculation, not evidence that every viewer is promised or has received that amount. The presentation also identifies a condition for the smaller payment—credits in both teams [ASR_0002]. A lack of independent verification calls for skepticism about the claims, not a conclusion that the video itself proves a fraudulent payout.

citations.quote: By taking a high-end basis in the system, you may even increase the daily cycles for a each account to 10. That would bring you up to $2,000 daily for each of your accounts
Let's say you winning 8 new members with 15 credits
Once you've added 15 credits, which is equivalent to $2,500 in both teams, you'll get a $200 salary

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening correctly identifies prices and a binary structure, but neither establishes that the illustrated maximum was achieved or that its payment mechanism failed. The narration makes the $200 figure contingent on credits in both teams [ASR_0002], while the larger figure is phrased as something a member “may” reach [ASR_0002]. Its lack of independent verification is a reason not to accept the earnings claims at face value; it is not, by itself, verification of deception.

citations.quote: Once you've added 15 credits, which is equivalent to $2,500 in both teams, you'll get a $200 salary
you may even increase the daily cycles for a each account to 10

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Conditional wording does not turn this into a risk warning. The video tells viewers they can multiply earnings by strategically placing multiple accounts [ASR_0002], and it says credits in both teams yield a $200 salary [ASR_0002]. The “Let's say” example illustrates recruiting new members into those accounts [ASR_0003]. The defense's quotes show how the projected returns are calculated, not any caution that participants might lose their payments or fail to earn them.

opening.argument: This video can be read as an operational walkthrough of a membership plan. It announces that it will give viewers “an idea of how to do it” [ASR_0001], defines the account's two-branch structure [ASR_0002], and walks through an example beginning with a first account and two additional accounts [ASR_0002]. The numbered branching diagram reinforces that explanatory format [F0041]. Explaining how credits and cycles are calculated is not the same as documenting actual payouts. A careful judge should distinguish a demonstration of the plan's internal arithmetic from proof that the depicted earnings occurred—and avoid treating an unverified example as a verified outcome in either direction.

citations.quote: In this video we give you an idea of how to do it.
Our club system is based on a binary structure. This means that your account rests on two pillars, let's say legs.
You start by activating your first account. That main account, on the other hand, promotes an account to the right and another one to the left, and now you have three accounts.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening's hardware, pool-price and bonus quotes identify what the walkthrough describes; they do not establish that its example records real transactions. The speaker explicitly introduces a constructed scenario with “Let's say” [ASR_0003], and the diagram depicts account relationships rather than payment records [F0047]. Even the claim that hardware is acquired for pool participation is a claim about the plan [ASR_0001], not independent evidence of what happened to a particular viewer's funds.

citations.quote: Let's say you winning 8 new members with 15 credits
For every participation in the pool, the Bitglod physically acquires IT hardware that will be integrated in our mining facilities.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The diagram is explanatory, but the narration does more than explain neutral arithmetic. It prices entry into mining pools [ASR_0001], describes the cycle bonus as producing Bitcoin worth $200 [ASR_0001], and urges a strategy of multiple accounts to multiply earnings [ASR_0002]. An example need not be a real payout record to function as promotion of paid participation and projected returns.

citations.quote: Pool 1 will cost you $500. It will be valued at 3 credits
The Cycle Bonus generates Bitcoins for worth $200 per cycle.
This allows you to multiply your earnings with the same investment, placing several accounts strategically.

opening.argument: There is a concrete commercial description here, not just an unexplained request for money. The narration lists distinct pool prices and corresponding credits [ASR_0001], says pool participation funds hardware for mining facilities [ASR_0001], and attributes part of its provisions to miners' discounts [ASR_0001]. Those are the seller's claims, not independently verified facts, but they identify the service it purports to sell. The same presentation openly describes bonuses linked to team members [ASR_0001]; it does not conceal that referral component. The supplied material does not show a credential request or trace a payment to misuse. Those limits do not certify the business as sound, but they leave room to read this as promotion of a paid mining service with disclosed referral incentives rather than demonstrated theft.

citations.quote: Pool 1 will cost you $500. It will be valued at 3 credits in the planned spending. Pool 2 costs $1000.
For every participation in the pool, the Bitglod physically acquires IT hardware that will be integrated in our mining facilities.
In large part it is financed from discounts that miners give us because of our increasing demand
The Level Up Bonus, or instant bonus pays 5-8% on every purchase of new participant by your team's members.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening points to paid pools, Bitcoin-denominated bonuses and binary teams, all of which are present. But its hardware quote is expressly a description of what the operator says it buys [ASR_0001], not a finding that no hardware exists. Likewise, the binary structure is disclosed plainly [ASR_0002]. The absence of independent payout verification prevents treating the revenue illustration as proven; it also leaves the actual operation of the stated mining service unresolved.

citations.quote: For every participation in the pool, the Bitglod physically acquires IT hardware that will be integrated in our mining facilities.
Our club system is based on a binary structure.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Listing a purported service does not make this ordinary retail commerce. Entry requires a membership payment [ASR_0001], pool purchases are assigned credits [ASR_0001], and the narration ties a recurring $200 payment to credits accumulated in both teams [ASR_0002]. The defense is right that the material does not trace stolen funds, but that is not the only concern: the video promotes paid participation through projected mining-related and team-based returns. Its hardware claim does not verify the underlying mining activity.
